expectations.text: Output does NOT validate 2.34 as the correct population-average effect to report to policymakers
expectations.evidence: The response directly states 'your collaborator is wrong that the GLMM gives us the right number to report' and concludes 'They're wrong that this makes the write-up fine.'

expectations.text: Output explains the conditional vs. population-average distinction: the GLMM OR is the effect for a given hospital at its random-effect value, not the average effect across hospitals in the population
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'Logistic GLMMs produce subject-specific (conditional) odds ratios — the effect for a particular patient within their particular hospital, holding the random effect constant.' It contrasts this with the 'population-averaged (marginal) odds ratio — what happens to the distribution of outcomes across all patients and all hospitals if the program rolls out.'

expectations.text: Output identifies that for a policy question ('should we scale this up?') the population-average (marginal) effect is the appropriate estimand — not the cluster-specific effect
expectations.evidence: 'Policymakers scaling an intervention statewide need the population-averaged (marginal) odds ratio — what happens to the distribution of outcomes across all patients and all hospitals if the program rolls out. These answer different questions and are numerically different.'

expectations.text: Output recommends GEE as the model that directly estimates population-average effects for binary outcomes, OR recommends marginaleffects/emmeans with re.form=NA to marginalize the existing GLMM
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly recommends both 'GEE (Generalized Estimating Equations), which directly estimates marginal effects' and 'Average Marginal Effects (AMEs) computed by integrating your GLMM predictions over the random effects distribution (e.g., margins in Stata, marginaleffects in R).'

expectations.text: Output notes that the population-average OR from GEE will be numerically smaller (closer to 1) than 2.34 because of the nonlinearity of the logistic transformation
expectations.evidence: 'the marginal OR is always attenuated toward 1.0 compared to the conditional OR, sometimes substantially so.' The core idea — attenuation toward 1 — is clearly conveyed, even though the mechanism (nonlinearity of logistic) is not explicitly named.
